P1.evidence: Setter notes genuinely read back, and specifically enough that the prospect corrected the detail: 'I spoke with Kim, that you had a call with him, I think, yesterday, right?... he briefed me in on your situation a little bit. But I'm an old goat... I would love to hear it from you... Because I understand that you've been into bodybuilding heavily, but you're looking for something else right now, correct?' Strong open question attached. No four-part frame and no frame agreement, which shows up later — the prospect ran the last fifteen minutes of the call, setting his own timeline and his own next steps.

P2.evidence: The injury and limitation work is the best in the batch. 'Do you have anything like any injuries or something that limits your movements?' surfaced the thoracic nerve damage, and the rep then chased the squat properly — ankles, depth, whether it is painful or unstable — and asked for a live demonstration on camera. Work was worked ('You sit a lot during the day?') and the career change explored at length. Nutrition was opened cleanly and the alcohol probe was well judged. But P2c is a clear miss with a concrete cost: health conditions were never asked as a question, and as a result the fact that this prospect had undergone surgery 20 days earlier and was under a lifting restriction did not emerge until 00:48:13, forty-five minutes later, and only because he volunteered it as an afterthought. Age, height and weight were all volunteered. Training frequency, sleep and daily energy were never raised at all.

P3.evidence: Nearly complete. The superficial goal was separated out cleanly ('Is there any, I would say, superficial kind of goal? Like, do you want to lose weight? Or that's on point?'). The can't-do question was asked properly and produced running, tennis and standing. The becoming-possible question was asked in the right form: 'when you have more mobility... what's becoming possible? What have you been putting on a backburner that you cannot do right now?' And the reflect-back is the second best in the batch: 'from what I'm hearing, you're not fighting for the looks. You're fighting just to finally stop feeling bad', which the prospect confirmed and sharpened — 'Tight and tired of standing... That's definitely priority number one.' The rep also connected the goal to the prospect's future identity as a surgeon standing in a lead vest, which was a genuinely good instinct. Only the who-else-does-this-impact question is entirely absent.

P4.evidence: What he had tried and what it did to him both emerged, but from the prospect's opening monologue rather than from questions — bodybuilding-style isolation work, feeling tighter after training than before, nerve damage from lifting too heavily. The rep never asked why it did not work, never asked what is actually in the way, and never had him name the gap. The prospect eventually named it himself at 00:37:46 — 'I think that's the biggest thing I want as well, structure, and form coaching, so I don't injure myself' — nearly forty minutes in and entirely unprompted. That sentence is the sale, and it arrived by luck.

P5.evidence: Two consequence statements were made and both were assertions rather than questions — 'you're only 25. That would like fast forward 20 years later. That definitely, that's gonna have a toll' and 'if you don't do anything about it, it's going to only get worse.' Then the rep explicitly withdrew: 'I don't want to, like, paint any more morbid picture for you, because you already know that you need to do something, yeah?... Let's paint a positive picture.' That is a deliberate abandonment of the phase, and it matches the coaching his manager delivered an hour after this call ended. Whether or not the coaching is right, the effect here was that a prospect who could not hold a deep squat at 25 and had already damaged a nerve left the call without ever being asked what two more years of this looks like or whether he is willing to settle for it.

P6.evidence: The belief question was asked well but in the wrong place — at 00:44:09, after the price and as an objection-handling move rather than as a gate before presenting: 'do you feel that what we've actually gone through today can actually get you to the body that you want?' Before the presentation the rep did not ask for commitment, he assumed it: 'So as you said, commitment for you is not an issue. So if you can figure out all the details, I can only assume that you will show up and you're going to be committed.' Assuming a yes is the weakest possible form of this check, and it produced no yes at all — the prospect's actual answer to the belief question, when it finally came, was the hedge 'Yeah, I think so' followed immediately by 'I just feel like, I don't know, it's expensive.'

P11.evidence: No close reached. The prospect declined the six-month, twelve-month and improvised one-month options and left with his own next steps.

objection_plays.detail: The best-run play in the batch, and it still only got halfway. The first three moves ran close to script: 'do you feel that what we've actually gone through today can actually get you to the body that you want?', then 'What makes you feel it can?', then 'what's coming up with the uncertainty part?' He also isolated properly — 'is it the money or is it you're a little bit uncertain still?' — and got 'maybe both', which is the answer that tells you to keep going. He then stopped. None of the closing moves ran: no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', no version of the identity move. Instead he offered a cheaper entry point and, when that was declined too, said 'Look, I understand it's a no.'

Trigger was explicit and quantified: 'grand a month... really nice gym membership is probably a third of that.' The rep isolated correctly and twice invited the financial conversation — 'money is just logistics, we can talk about it' and 'can we talk numbers? Because if this is the thing about the numbers, we can talk about it' — which is more than he managed on the Luke Charleston call. The prospect declined both times, so none of the financial-picture questions ran: no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments. The value reframe was decent ('you're not buying a gym membership. You're not buying a PT here') but it asserted rather than demonstrated, and the payment plan was mentioned correctly with interest attached and then never structured.

A third-party consult trigger in a non-spousal form: 'I want to talk to friends that are in sort of like the fitness space and make sure this is something they think is worth this much money.' The rep ran the closest applicable move — 'How can your friends actually help you with the decision?' — which is the right challenge, and then let it go when the prospect deflected with 'Who knows, man? You don't know until you ask.' None of the follow-through ran: no 'what obstacles might come up when you talk to them', no 'is this genuinely needing their input or asking permission to bet on yourself', no deposit-and-refund offer.

Clear trigger at 00:47:27 — moving apartments in two weeks, travelling until then, 'I don't even really think I'd be ready to start until like at least July 20th.' The play did not run at all. No 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets — metabolism slows, injuries compound', which was tailor-made here for a 25-year-old with documented nerve damage and a squat he cannot hold. The rep answered only that the first month is learning movements, which minimised the objection rather than dissolving it.

A free-substitute trigger with no scripted play: the prospect is already doing the product's own free YouTube content and named consuming more of it as his next step — 'I just want to do a little bit more of my own research on his YouTube before I commit.' His verdict on the paid programme was 'it sounds pretty standard.' The rep did make one relevant argument at 00:37:03, that unstructured YouTube work stalls people at six to eight months, but never returned to it once the free content resurfaced as the actual alternative. When the product's own marketing channel is the competitor, the script has nothing.

notes: Strongest goals work and strongest injury questioning in the batch, and the deal still died on the two things that were skipped. P2c was never asked, so a 20-day post-surgical restriction surfaced by accident in the fifty-first minute. P5 was deliberately abandoned mid-frame, so a prospect with a vividly described problem was never asked what it costs to leave it. Coach the sequencing: the belief question belongs before the price, not as a rescue after it.
